title: 2026 property tax levy and special service levies approved
subtitle: Also: new artist grant policy, sustainability update, deposit-return call to Ontario, and reservist policy recognition.
overview: Council set the 2026 general tax levy at a final municipal amount of $114,461,396 and passed the by-law that governs payment of 2026 property taxes {{vote:m5}}. Council also approved special service levies for five homes associations to fund their recreation facilities and programs {{vote:m6}}. The mayor and one councillor stepped out for that item because of a declared conflict of interest.

Council approved a new Artists in Neighbourhoods Grant Policy {{vote:m3}} and received a sustainability and climate change status update {{vote:m7}}. Staff reported on progress under the city's climate plans and the 10,000 Trees for Waterloo project, and said greenhouse gas emissions reporting for 2024 and 2025 will return in the fall. Council also asked the Province of Ontario to bring in a deposit-return program for non-alcoholic beverage containers {{vote:m8}}.

The meeting began with a closed session on land disposition and utility enterprise matters. The minutes report no public decisions from it. Council also received a "With Glowing Hearts" certificate recognizing the city's reservist policy. A motion asking the province to fund heritage building reuse for housing was tabled for consideration on April 27.

decisions.detail: Council approved the report and adopted the 2026 General Tax Levy By-law based on a final municipal levy of $114,461,396.
Council approved levies on five homes associations' areas to fund operating and capital costs of their recreation facilities and programs, and approved the related by-law.
Council approved report COM2026-012 and the new M-017 Artists in Neighbourhoods Grant Policy.
Council called on Ontario to implement a deposit-return program for non-alcoholic beverage containers and to send the motion to provincial officials, AMO and other municipalities.
Council received the status report as information, including the 2025 sustainability updates and tree planting progress.
Council received the report on 2025 tax adjustments as information.

debate: Staff said greenhouse gas emissions reporting moved to the fall so it can include both 2024 and 2025 data. This also narrows the usual two-year lag and leaves time to develop a clearer public reporting format.
A councillor asked that the fall report come back with updates on the Uptown sustainability recommendations. Another asked for more detail on what is committed and complete, and on timelines.

Asked about 13 paused climate actions, staff said reasons include limited staff capacity or expertise, new legislation, shifting community priorities, and projects proving larger than expected. Paused actions will be reassessed.

On pedestrian crossovers, staff said at least three are planned this year. Rising costs mean a staged approach over several years, and automated speed camera revenue could fund more once the amount is known.

In moving the deposit-return motion, a councillor said Ontario lags other provinces in container recovery. The councillor cited the burden of waste on the Great Lakes and said provincial leadership is needed as recycling rates fluctuate.
